0.title: Waiting for His Son from Heaven
0.overview:
First Thessalonians is the earliest letter Paul wrote that has been preserved in the New Testament — penned from Corinth around AD 50–51, within just weeks or months of his departure from the Thessalonian church. It is a letter warm with affection, urgent with concern, and radiant with hope. More than almost any other letter in the Pauline corpus, it vibrates with the pulse of a young church under pressure and a pastor who loves them like a father, a mother, and a brother all at once.

The city of Thessalonica was the capital of the Roman province of Macedonia — a major port, a commercial hub, a city full of every religion Rome and the East could offer. Paul had arrived there on his second missionary journey, preached for perhaps three weeks in the synagogue, and watched as a community of faith was born — Jewish converts, god-fearing Greeks, and not a few prominent women (Acts 17:1–9). Then a riot broke out, the city authorities were alarmed, and Paul was smuggled out by night. He never forgot those he had left behind.

The letter's great themes weave together like threads in a tapestry. There is the gospel — how it arrived in Thessalonica not merely as words but in power, in the Holy Spirit, in full conviction (1:5). There is the church as a community shaped by faith, hope, and love — Paul's great triad appears here earlier than in 1 Corinthians 13. There is holiness — the call to sanctification, especially in the realm of sexual purity, that flies directly in the face of Greco-Roman culture. And there is the return of Christ — the parousia — which dominates the last two chapters and gives the whole letter its eschatological urgency. The Thessalonians were grieving for those who had died before Jesus returned; Paul's answer is the most vivid description of the Second Coming in all of Scripture.

Above all, this is a letter about hope. Not the vague optimism the world calls hope, but the taut, muscular, resurrection-grounded hope that transforms how believers grieve, how they work, how they treat their bodies, and how they face the future. 'We do not want you to be uninformed, brothers, about those who are asleep,' Paul writes, 'so that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope' (4:13). That contrast — hope versus hopelessness — is the heartbeat of 1 Thessalonians. The God who raised Jesus will raise them. The Lord who ascended will descend. The church that suffers now will be presented blameless before him at his coming.

1.title: The Gospel That Works
1.overview:
The first chapter of 1 Thessalonians is a cascade of gratitude. Paul looks back at what happened in Thessalonica and can barely contain himself: a gospel arrived, a church was born, and that church became a blazing testimony that lit up the whole of Macedonia and Achaia. In just thirteen verses Paul sketches what authentic gospel ministry looks like — from both the preacher's side and the hearer's side — and the portrait is breathtaking in its simplicity and power.

The Thessalonians had received the word in much affliction, with joy inspired by the Holy Spirit (v. 6). That combination — affliction and joy together — is the signature of Spirit-wrought faith. They had turned from idols to serve the living and true God. They were waiting for his Son from heaven. And the whole region knew it. Paul hadn't needed to say a word about Thessalonica when he travelled on; the Thessalonians' reputation had run ahead of him. Their faith had gone forth. The gospel, once received, had become a gospel proclaimed.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The shortest opening Paul ever wrote, and every omission tells. No apostolic title — where his authority is contested he insists on it, and here he does not need to. Just three names: Paul, Silvanus (the Silas who was chained beside him in the Philippian jail), and Timothy, all three of whom had worked in Thessalonica together.

The address carries the weight. Not the church at Thessalonica, as though the city defined them, but the church in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. A few dozen recent converts, meeting in a house in a town that had just driven their teacher out by night, are told where they actually live. And the two names stand under one preposition, Father and Lord together, with no explanation offered — which from a man raised on the Shema is a remarkable thing to do by instinct rather than argument.

Then grace and peace, in the only order they come in: grace the unearned favour that comes down, peace what it makes when it lands.
verseByVerse.theology:
Joining the Father and the Lord Jesus as a single source of grace and peace is a compressed Christology, and its date is what makes it startling. This letter is very likely the earliest document in the New Testament, written around twenty years after the crucifixion — well before any Gospel. There was no long development during which a human teacher was gradually elevated to divine status. The highest view of Christ is already here, in the first line of the first thing written, stated as though it needed no defence.

The Reformed tradition, with Nicaea, has always insisted that a creature cannot be a co-source of divine blessing. Grace and peace come from God; if they come from Jesus in the same breath and under the same preposition, then Jesus is not on the creature side of the line. The greeting is a doxology in miniature: two persons, one blessing.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: In Thessalonica, kyrios was Caesar title, and the city was proud of its standing with Rome — a free city that had backed the winning side and kept its own assembly for it. Acts records the charge laid against these believers exactly: they say there is another king, Jesus (Acts 17:7). To receive a letter greeting them from the Lord Jesus was to be reminded whose throne their welfare actually came from.

Now: Notice what Paul does not put in his greeting. No title, no credentials, no reminder of what he had done for them. Where he was loved and trusted he simply used his name. It is a small thing, and it is a fair question for anyone who holds office in a church: how much of your authority do you find you have to keep asserting, and why?

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, To the church of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: Grace to you and peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before anything else, know how young this church was. Paul had come to Thessalonica from Philippi, where he had been beaten with rods and jailed, and he reasoned in the synagogue there on three Sabbath days (Acts 17:2). Some weeks later a mob dragged his host before the magistrates and the believers sent Paul away by night. Perhaps a month, perhaps a little more. Then he was gone, and these people were on their own in a hostile city with almost no teaching and no apostle.

This letter, written a few months afterwards from Corinth, is very likely the earliest thing in the New Testament. Nothing else we possess was written down first. And what it contains is not a treatise but the relief of a man who had been frantic with worry about a congregation he had been forced to abandon.

Notice what is missing from the opening. Paul does not call himself an apostle. In Galatians the first line insists on it, because his authority was under attack there; to the Corinthians the same. Here, nothing — just his name, alongside two others. Where he is loved and trusted, he does not need the title, and he does not use it. That is worth observing in a man often accused of high-handedness.

Silvanus is the Silas of Acts, the man who was chained beside Paul in the Philippian jail and sang at midnight; Timothy is the young man from Lystra who will be sent back to Thessalonica alone, at some risk, in chapter 3. All three had been in the city together. Paul writes as one of a team, and he means it.

Then the address, and one small preposition carries a great deal: the church of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Not the church at Thessalonica, as though the city were what defined them. They are located in God. A scattering of ex-idolaters and synagogue attenders, weeks old, meeting in somebody's house in a town that had just run their teacher out — and Paul tells them where they actually live.

And the two names are joined under one preposition, the Father and the Lord Jesus together, without a word of explanation. No Jew raised on the Shema does that casually. This is one of the earliest sentences in the New Testament and it already places Jesus on the divine side of the line, not by argument but by instinct.

Grace and peace. The order never varies and cannot. Grace is the unearned favour that comes down; peace is what it makes when it lands. A church under pressure needs both, and in that order.

verseByVerse.ref: 1:2–10 – Faith, Love, Hope — and a Church Everyone Was Talking About
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul gives thanks always, for all of them, constantly (v.2) — and then names what he gives thanks for, in the triad that may be appearing here for the first time in Christian writing: their work of faith, labour of love, and steadfastness of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ (v.3). Each virtue is measured by what it produces.

From that fruit he draws a conclusion about the root: he knows they are loved by God and chosen (v.4) — and the word because takes him straight to his evidence. The gospel came to them not only in word but in power, in the Holy Spirit, and with full conviction; and they had seen for themselves what kind of men the messengers proved to be among them (v.5).

So they became imitators of Paul and of the Lord in one specific respect — receiving the word in much affliction with the joy of the Holy Spirit (v.6) — and by that became a stamped example to every believer in Macedonia and Achaia (v.7). From them the word of the Lord has sounded out like a struck bell, their faith reported everywhere, so that Paul finds he need say nothing (v.8).

What people report is the shape of their conversion: they turned to God from idols, to serve the living and true God (v.9), and to wait for his Son from heaven, whom God raised from the dead — Jesus who delivers them from the wrath to come (v.10).
verseByVerse.theology:
Election, and How Anyone Could Know

Verse 4 states election flatly and warmly, and verse 5 gives the grounds. Paul claims no private glimpse of the eternal register. He reasons from effect to cause: the gospel arrived among these people with power, the Spirit, and settled conviction, and it produced work, labour and endurance — therefore God had chosen them. The hidden decree becomes visible in time through the effectual call. Calvin put it exactly: we know our election by our calling.

Two guards keep this from going wrong. Their faith and love are not the ground of their election — that lies wholly in God — but they are the evidence of it; fruit confirming a root nobody can dig up and inspect. And notice the pastoral use Paul makes of the doctrine. He does not deploy it to sort the congregation or to threaten. He hands it to persecuted people as the one piece of ground that cannot shift: if your standing rested on the firmness of your own decision, a hard enough season could undo it; resting on his choice, it cannot.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Thessalonica was the provincial capital, and its religion was civic rather than private. Trade guilds met at sacrificial meals under patron gods; households kept their own deities; loyalty to Rome was expressed in the imperial cult. To turn from idols was not a change of opinion but resignation from the life of the town, which is precisely why affliction followed (v.6). And the whole thing happened fast: Paul had perhaps a month in the city (Acts 17:2) before a mob forced him out at night, yet within months this church was the pattern held up to older congregations across two provinces.

Now: Verse 3 supplies a test worth running, because faith, love and hope cost nothing to claim. Paul measures each by its output — work, exhaustion, staying put. Ask not whether you have them but whether anything in your week would look different if you did not. And verse 9 gives the useful form of the idol question: since ours are rarely carved, asking whether you own any statues settles nothing. Ask what you serve — what the week is organised around, what you are most afraid of losing, what you would trade sleep and integrity to keep.

verseByVerse.quote: We give thanks to God always for all of you, constantly mentioning you in our prayers,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three words govern this verse and each is worth weighing: always, all, constantly.

We give thanks to God always. Paul had left this church in the worst possible circumstances and had spent the intervening months, as chapter 3 will tell us, unable to bear the suspense and half-convinced his labour had been wasted. Thanksgiving was not his obvious response to Thessalonica. It was his settled one.

For all of you. Not for the promising ones or the ones who had held up best under pressure. All. Paul writes to five congregations elsewhere that he has to correct, and even there he thanks God for the whole body before he says anything else.

Constantly mentioning you in our prayers. The word means unceasingly, without a gap — and Paul uses it four times in this short letter, more than anywhere else he writes. He is describing a habit, not a mood: this church came up every time he prayed, because he could not stop thinking about them.

There is a plain lesson here that most of us need more than we need a new doctrine. Paul is worried sick about these people and cannot reach them. What he does with the worry is turn it into thanksgiving and intercession. He does not brood, and he does not wait until the news is good. Anxiety about people you love is raw material; Paul shows you what to do with it.

verseByVerse.quote: remembering before our God and Father your work of faith and labor of love and steadfastness of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the triad that will become famous — faith, love, hope — and this is very likely the first time it was ever written down. But look at what Paul attaches to each, because the nouns are doing the real work: the work of faith, the labour of love, the steadfastness of hope.

Faith produces work. Not work that earns anything — Paul will spend Romans and Galatians demolishing that — but work that faith itself generates, as a live root pushes up a shoot. A faith that has changed nothing about what you do is a faith Paul would not recognise.

Love produces labour. The word is kopos, and it is not light work. It means toil to the point of exhaustion, the sweat of a man at the end of a long day. Paul does not say love produces warm feeling. He says it produces the kind of tiredness you get from doing something hard for somebody else. Most real love in a church looks like being worn out by people.

Hope produces steadfastness. Hypomone — not passive resignation but the quality of a man who stays under a weight without buckling. And note the direction: hope is what makes endurance possible, not the other way round. You can bear almost anything if you know it ends and how. These people were being persecuted; Paul tells them their staying power is fed by what is coming.

Then the anchor for all three: in our Lord Jesus Christ. The phrase governs the whole line. This is not a list of admirable human qualities; it is a description of what Christ produces in people joined to him.

And there is a test in the verse for anyone who wants one. Faith, love and hope are easy words and cost nothing to claim. Paul measures them by what they produce — work, exhaustion, staying put. Ask not whether you have them but whether anything in your week would be different if you did not.

verseByVerse.quote: For we know, brothers loved by God, that he has chosen you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two enormous things are said here almost in passing, and Paul says them to a church perhaps six months old.

First: brothers loved by God. The construction is a perfect passive participle — having been loved, and standing loved. It is not a description of how God feels about them on a good day. It is a settled state they are in.

Second: he has chosen you. The word is election, and Paul states it flatly, without hedging or apology, as a comfort rather than a puzzle. This is the doctrine some Christians find cold, and it is worth noticing where Paul puts it: in a letter to frightened people under persecution, as the first solid ground he can give them. If your standing rested on your own decision, a bad enough month could undo it. If it rests on his choice, it cannot.

But the question the verse actually raises is the one people ask in the car park afterwards: how could Paul know? Election is a decree made in eternity, and no one has read the register. Paul is not claiming a private revelation. He tells us his evidence in the next word — because — and it runs straight into verse 5: he knows they were chosen because of how the gospel arrived among them.

That is the pastoral shape of the doctrine, and it is the answer to the person who lies awake wondering whether he is one of them. You do not find out by trying to read God's mind. You look for the effects: a word that landed with power, a life that turned, a love for people you did not use to love, a persistence you cannot account for in yourself. Calvin said it plainly — we know our election by our calling. The root is hidden; the fruit is not.

And note the tone. Paul does not use election to sort the congregation into sheep and goats, and he does not brandish it as a threat. He uses it the way you would use a deed of title with a nervous tenant: this is yours, and here is why nobody can take it.

verseByVerse.quote: because our gospel came to you not only in word, but also in power and in the Holy Spirit and with full conviction. You know what kind of men we proved to be among you for your sake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is Paul's evidence, and it has two halves. The gospel came to them not only in word — the word was necessary and there was no gospel without it — but also in power and in the Holy Spirit and with full conviction.

Take that seriously and it reorders how we think about preaching. Words are the instrument; they are not the agent. Paul was as capable a speaker as the early church had, and he refuses to credit the result to his own delivery. The same sermon can be preached twice and leave one room unmoved and another in tears, and the difference is not the sermon.

Full conviction translates plerophoria, a word for something carried all the way to completion — settled, unhesitating certainty. Not that they found the argument persuasive. That the thing landed on them with the weight of fact.

Then the second half of the verse, and it is the half most often skipped: You know what kind of men we proved to be among you for your sake. Paul does not stop at the Spirit's power; he points to the messengers themselves, and to what these people had watched with their own eyes.

What had they watched? Men who arrived with their backs still marked from a flogging in Philippi (2:2), who worked night and day at a trade so as not to burden anybody (2:9), and who left town under cover of darkness rather than get their converts killed. The gospel did not come to Thessalonica as a lecture. It came in the hands of men whose lives corroborated it, and Paul says so — for your sake, because even that was aimed at them, not at his own reputation.

Hold the two halves together and you have Paul's whole doctrine of how the gospel travels. The Spirit gives the power; a life gives the credibility. Neither substitutes for the other. A blameless life without the word saves nobody, and the word from a life that contradicts it will be weighed and dismissed, and rightly.

verseByVerse.quote: And you became imitators of us and of the Lord, for you received the word in much affliction, with the joy of the Holy Spirit, so that you became an example to all the believers in Macedonia and in Achaia.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They became imitators of Paul and of the Lord — and Paul immediately says in what respect, because otherwise the claim is impossibly vague. They imitated him in this: you received the word in much affliction, with the joy of the Holy Spirit. That is the point of resemblance. Not his gifts, not his knowledge. The way he took a beating and kept his joy.

And they had seen him do it. These people had watched Paul arrive with his back marked from Philippi and preach anyway; some of them had watched him hustled out of town at night. Then the same trouble came on them, and they behaved the same way. Imitation in the New Testament is rarely about copying a technique. It is about having watched somebody under pressure and finding, when your turn comes, that you do what they did.

Hold the two halves of the phrase together, because either one alone is a different religion. In much affliction — real trouble, not inconvenience; the word is thlipsis, pressure, the crushing weight. With the joy of the Holy Spirit — and note whose joy it is. Not joy they worked up, and not the absence of pain. Something the Spirit produced in them while the pressure was still on.

That combination is the thing the watching world cannot explain, and it is why the next sentence follows. Affliction without joy is simply misfortune and nobody remarks on it. Joy without affliction is cheap and proves nothing. Joy inside affliction is a fact that demands an explanation, and people go looking for one.

So they became an example to all the believers in Macedonia and in Achaia. The word is typos — the mark left by a blow, a die, a stamp; our word type. They had been struck by the gospel and now carried its impression, and other churches could read it off them.

Weigh how quickly this happened. Paul had been with them a matter of weeks. He is writing months later, and already this congregation of new converts is the pattern being held up to the older, better-taught churches of two Roman provinces — Macedonia to the north, Achaia to the south, which included Athens and Corinth. Length of time in the faith and usefulness to God are not the same measurement.

verseByVerse.quote: For not only has the word of the Lord sounded forth from you in Macedonia and Achaia, but your faith in God has gone forth everywhere, so that we need not say anything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The verb is the striking thing. The word of the Lord has sounded forth from you — exechetai, from which we get echo. It is used of a trumpet blast and of thunder rolling out. The picture is not of missionaries dispatched but of a sound that carries: the gospel struck this church like a hammer on a bell, and the ringing went out across the province.

And the tense matters — it is perfect, meaning it sounded and is still sounding. Paul is not describing a campaign that finished. He is describing a noise that has not yet stopped.

Then he widens it further: your faith in God has gone forth everywhere. Thessalonica sat on the Via Egnatia, the great Roman road that ran across Macedonia from the Adriatic to Byzantium, and it was a busy port. Travellers, traders and sailors passed through constantly, and they carried the story with them. The church did not organise this. They simply lived in a city everybody went through.

Then a line with a smile in it: so that we need not say anything. Paul, whose entire vocation was saying things, arrives somewhere to talk about the gospel and finds the ground already covered. People tell him about the Thessalonians before he can tell them. He is delighted to be redundant.

There is something bracing here for ordinary Christians who feel they have no gift for this. What travelled was not a programme or an argument. It was a report — that a group of people in Thessalonica had dropped their idols and would not stop being glad about it under pressure. Nobody in that church set out to be famous across two provinces. They were simply visible, and what could be seen was worth repeating.

Which raises the uncomfortable question in the other direction. Every church has a reputation in its town, and it is never the one printed on the noticeboard. It is whatever the neighbours say when the subject comes up. What is sounding forth from yours?

verseByVerse.quote: For they themselves report concerning us the kind of reception we had among you, and how you turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul now quotes what other people are saying, and it turns out to be one of the compact summaries of conversion in the New Testament. Two movements: a turning from, and a turning to.

You turned to God from idols. Note the order in which Paul reports it — toward God first, and from idols as the consequence. That is nearly always the actual sequence. People rarely put down an idol because they have been persuaded it is worthless in the abstract; they put it down because something better has taken hold of them. Try to reverse it and you get willpower, which is a short-lived fuel.

And understand what it cost in that city. Thessalonica was the provincial capital, thick with the worship of Dionysus, Serapis and Cabirus, and — most dangerously — with the imperial cult. Religion there was not a private preference. It was civic membership: the trade guilds had patron gods and their meetings were sacrificial meals, family life ran on household deities, and public loyalty was measured by attendance. To turn from idols was to resign from the life of the town. It explains the affliction of verse 6 entirely.

To serve the living and true God. Both adjectives are aimed. An idol is not living — it is wood and stone, and Isaiah mocked the man who fells a tree, burns half for warmth and worships the other half. And it is not true — it does not correspond to anything. Paul is using the language of Jeremiah, who called the LORD the living God and the true God (Jer 10:10) against exactly such rivals.

The verb serve is douleuein, to serve as a slave. That is a blunt word for what they turned to, and it is deliberate. They did not exchange servitude for independence. They changed owners. The question a person faces is never whether to serve something but which master is worth it — and only one of the available masters is alive.

Which puts the question to us in the only form that is any use. Our idols are rarely carved, so asking whether you own any statues settles nothing. Ask instead what you serve: what you organise your week around, what you are afraid of losing, what you would sacrifice sleep and money and integrity to keep. That is the altar, whatever is or is not standing on it.

verseByVerse.quote: and to wait for his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead, Jesus who delivers us from the wrath to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The report has one more clause, and it is the one that shapes the rest of the letter: they turned to wait for his Son from heaven. Two verbs describe the Christian life here, and both are present and continuous — to serve, and to wait. Work and watch. Neither without the other.

The waiting is not idleness; the word carries expectancy, watching a road. And remember how new these believers were. Within weeks of conversion they had been taught to live with their eyes on the horizon — so much so that by chapter 4 they are anxious about what happens to those who die before he arrives. Paul had evidently told them a great deal in a very short time.

Then the grounds for expecting him at all: whom he raised from the dead. The return is not a hope hanging in mid-air. It rests on something that already happened in public. A man who has been raised is a man who can come back.

And then the last clause, which needs handling with care: Jesus who delivers us from the wrath to come.

Modern readers flinch at wrath, often because they picture divine temper — God losing control. That is not the biblical idea. God's wrath is his settled, judicial opposition to evil, and a God who felt nothing about cruelty and injustice would not be good. We would not admire a judge who shrugged at atrocity. The wrath to come is the guarantee that the accounts of history will eventually be settled.

Note that Paul does not tell frightened persecuted people that wrath is coming for them. He tells them the opposite, and the tense is the comfort: Jesus delivers — present, ongoing, a rescue already in force. The wrath is future; the deliverance is a fact now. They are not hoping to escape. They have been taken out already, by the one who absorbed it himself.

So the chapter that began with three men and a greeting ends looking down the road. Turned, serving, waiting — past, present and future, and the whole Christian life inside ten verses.

2.title: A Nursing Mother and a Urging Father
2.overview:
Chapter 2 is Paul at his most personally transparent. Faced, apparently, with accusations that he had been a charlatan — a travelling sophist who preached for money and flattery and then abandoned his converts — Paul recounts his ministry in Thessalonica in intimate, pastoral detail. He is not being defensive in the manner of a wounded ego; he is being transparent in the manner of a man whose deepest identity is bound up with the Thessalonians' wellbeing.

The images he uses are extraordinary. He compares himself and his team to a nursing mother (v. 7) — giving not just the gospel but their very lives, tender and self-giving. Then he shifts: they were like a father urging and encouraging and charging each one of them to walk in a manner worthy of God (v. 11). Mother-tenderness and father-urgency together: the complete pastoral image. This is not sentimentality; it is Paul's theology of ministry made flesh.

The chapter also records his anguish at being separated from them — 'torn away from you' (v. 17), like a child snatched from a parent. Satan had hindered his return. But the Thessalonians themselves were his hope and joy and crown of boasting at the Lord's coming. The eschatological horizon of chapter 4 is already casting its light here: pastoral ministry is not just about the present but about that final day when pastor and congregation stand together before Jesus.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Something had been said about Paul after he left, and you can hear the accusation in what he denies. He begins with their own memory: their coming was not empty (v.1), and it came at a price — he had arrived still marked from the flogging at Philippi and preached with God-given boldness in the middle of conflict (v.2).

Three denials cover the three ways ministry goes wrong: not error in the message, not impurity in the motive, not deceit in the method (v.3) — because he speaks as a man tested and entrusted with a deposit, working for God's verdict rather than an audience's (v.4). Then the charges answered one by one: no flattery, and they are his witnesses; no pretext for greed, and God is his witness, since motives are invisible (v.5); no seeking of glory from anyone — though he could have made demands as an apostle (v.6).

What he was instead: gentle as a nursing mother with her own child (v.7), longing for them with a word found nowhere else in the Greek Bible, and ready to hand over not only the gospel but himself (v.8). And the hardest evidence of all — labour and toil, working night and day at a trade so as to be a burden to nobody while he preached (v.9).

He calls both courts to his conduct, theirs and God's: holy, righteous, blameless (v.10). Then the second family image — like a father with his children (v.11) — exhorting, encouraging and charging each one of them individually to walk worthy of the God who is calling them into his own kingdom and glory (v.12).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Minister as Steward, Not Owner

The governing idea of the passage is in verse 4: entrusted with the gospel. The word is used of a deposit placed in someone's keeping. It is not Paul's gospel, as though he had devised it — he is a courier carrying what belongs to another, and a courier does not edit the parcel. The Reformed tradition has always insisted the minister stands under the word rather than over it: a steward, never an entrepreneur.

Notice that Paul uses the assayer's word dokimazo twice in one sentence. He has been tested and approved; and he speaks before the God who goes on testing hearts. The examination is continuous, which is why the sentence lands where it does — not to please man, but to please God. This is not indifference to people; Paul has just described treating them with a nursing mother's tenderness. It is a question of whose verdict he is working for, and the two audiences pull apart at exactly the point where the true thing and the popular thing separate.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The circuit Paul travelled was worked by professional lecturers and religious salesmen who lived on their rhetoric, took what they could get, and moved on. The quickest way to destroy a young church was to persuade it that its founder had been one of them. So Paul answers with what could be checked: they had watched him arrive injured and preach anyway, and they had watched him at a leatherworker's bench before dawn and after dark so that none of them would have to pay for him.

Now: Verse 6 is the sharpest line for anyone holding office. Paul had the right to be supported and honoured, defends that right vigorously elsewhere (1 Cor 9:4-14), and declined to press it. The question in ministry — as in any relationship where one party holds the power — is almost never whether you have a right. Usually you do. It is what you intend to do with it. And verse 9 needs its guard: Paul is not ruling out paid ministry, which he explicitly upholds (1 Cor 9:14; and 5:12 below). He waived a fair claim in one place for one reason, so that nothing about money could stand between these people and the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: For you yourselves know, brothers, that our coming to you was not in vain. But though we had already suffered and been shamefully treated at Philippi, as you know, we had boldness in our God to declare to you the gospel of God in the midst of much conflict.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Something has been said about Paul in Thessalonica after he left, and this chapter is his answer. You can hear the shape of the accusation in what he denies: that he was a flatterer, that he was after money, that he was chasing a reputation, that he ran away when it got difficult. Travelling philosophers and religious salesmen worked that circuit constantly, took what they could get and moved on, and the easiest way to damage a young church was to persuade it that its founder had been another of them.

So Paul does not argue in the abstract. Four times in twelve verses he says some version of you know — you were there, you saw it. His defence is their own memory.

'Our coming to you was not in vain.' The word is kenos, empty — hollow, with nothing in it. It can describe an empty-handed visit or an empty-headed message. Paul means the whole enterprise had content and produced something, and the congregation reading the letter was the proof.

Then the detail that gives the sentence its weight: 'though we had already suffered and been shamefully treated at Philippi.' He is not being vague. In Philippi he and Silas had been stripped in the marketplace, beaten with rods, and put in the stocks — and they were Roman citizens, which made it illegal as well as brutal. That is what 'shamefully treated' means; the word carries insult, not just injury. Thessalonica was the next stop, about a hundred miles down the road. He arrived still marked.

And preached anyway. 'We had boldness in our God' — parrhesia, the freedom to speak openly, the confidence of a man who says everything and hides nothing. Note where he sources it: in our God, not in his own nerve. This was borrowed courage, and Paul says so, which is the opposite of the boast he is accused of.

'In the midst of much conflict.' Agon — the contest, the struggle in the arena. Not conflict he encountered afterwards; conflict that was going on while he spoke. Acts tells us how it ended: a mob, a riot, and the believers getting him out of the city by night.

Set the two halves together and you have the argument of the whole chapter in miniature. A man in it for money or applause does not walk from a flogging in one city into a riot in the next. The cost is the credential.

verseByVerse.quote: For our appeal does not spring from error or impurity or any attempt to deceive, but just as we have been approved by God to be entrusted with the gospel, so we speak, not to please man, but to please God who tests our hearts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three denials, then the positive that explains them. 'Our appeal does not spring from error or impurity or any attempt to deceive.'

Take them one at a time, because they cover three different ways a ministry goes wrong. Error (plane) is about the message — a man may be sincere and simply wrong, wandering and taking others with him. Impurity (akatharsia) is about motive, and in this period the word carried a sexual edge; the mystery cults had a reputation, and a travelling teacher with access to households was a known hazard. Deceit (dolos) is about method — the word is used of baiting a hook. Wrong content, dirty motives, manipulative technique. Paul denies all three, and any one of them is enough to ruin a ministry that is sound in the other two.

Then the positive: 'just as we have been approved by God to be entrusted with the gospel, so we speak.' The verb behind 'approved' is dokimazo, the assayer's word for testing metal and finding it genuine. And Paul uses it twice in one sentence — he has been tested and passed, by the God who tests hearts. The examination is not over. It is continuous.

'Entrusted with the gospel' is the governing idea. The word is used of a deposit placed in someone's keeping. It is not Paul's gospel, as though he had thought of it; he is a courier carrying something that belongs to someone else, and a courier does not get to edit the parcel.

Which produces the sentence everything turns on: 'not to please man, but to please God who tests our hearts.' Notice this is not a claim to be indifferent to people — Paul has just spent verses describing how tenderly he treated them. It is a question of which verdict he is working for. And the two audiences pull in opposite directions constantly: one of them can be pleased by softening what is hard, and one of them sees the heart while you do it.

The test is a simple one and not comfortable. Every preacher, teacher and parent knows the moment when the true thing and the popular thing part company. What you do in that moment tells you which approval you are actually working for, whatever you would say you believe about it.

verseByVerse.quote: For we never came with words of flattery, as you know, nor with a pretext for greed—God is witness. Nor did we seek glory from people, whether from you or from others, though we could have made demands as apostles of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the three specific charges, and Paul answers each with a different kind of evidence.

'We never came with words of flattery, as you know.' Flattery is not simply kindness or encouragement. It is saying what a person wants to hear in order to get something from them — praise with a hook in it. The ancient moralists despised the flatterer precisely because he was a manipulator wearing a friend's face. And for this charge Paul appeals to their memory: you were there, you heard what I actually said.

'Nor with a pretext for greed — God is witness.' Here the evidence changes, and the change is exact. A pretext is a cover story: ministry used as a front for making money. But greed is a motive, and motives are invisible; the Thessalonians could not testify to what was in his heart. So Paul calls a witness who can. He does not ask them to take his word for what only God can see.

'Nor did we seek glory from people, whether from you or from others.' The third is subtler than money and more common among religious people. A man can be scrupulous about cash and still be feeding on being admired. And Paul widens it deliberately — not from you or from others. He is not merely saying he did not exploit the Thessalonians. He is saying he was not building a reputation to spend somewhere else.

Then the clause that lifts the whole passage: 'though we could have made demands as apostles of Christ.' He had the right. Apostles could claim support and honour, and Paul defends that right vigorously elsewhere (1 Cor 9:4-14) before saying he has never used it. So this is not a man without standing making a virtue of necessity. It is a man with every entitlement declining to press it.

Which is exactly the mind Paul describes in the great hymn: one who, being in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be exploited (Phil 2:6). The question in ministry, as in every relationship where one person holds power, is almost never whether you have a right. Usually you do. It is what you intend to do with the right you have.

verseByVerse.quote: But we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother taking care of her own children. So, being affectionately desirous of you, we were ready to share with you not only the gospel of God but also our own selves, because you had become very dear to us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having said what he was not, Paul says what he was — and reaches for an image no one would have expected from him. 'We were gentle among you, like a nursing mother taking care of her own children.'

The word for the nurse is trophos, and the phrase 'her own' is doing real work: not a hired wet-nurse minding somebody else's baby, but a mother feeding her own child from her own body. That is the picture — the most ordinary and most costly form of self-giving there is, and it happens at night, unseen, with no thanks and no audience.

There is a well-known textual question in this verse. The Greek manuscripts divide between epioi, gentle, and nepioi, infants — one letter apart, and in ancient copies written without word-spacing the preceding word ends in that letter, so the confusion is easy. If it is 'infants', Paul says he became a small child among them, which then shifts abruptly to the nursing mother in the same breath. Either reading tells against the charge of self-importance, and the ESV's 'gentle' gives the smoother sense.

Then the longing, in a word Paul uses nowhere else: 'being affectionately desirous of you' translates homeiromenoi, which appears in the Greek Bible only here and on a gravestone inscription, where grieving parents use it of a lost child. It is the ache of wanting someone you cannot reach. That is what this apostle felt about a church he had known for a month.

And then the sentence that defines pastoral work: 'we were ready to share with you not only the gospel of God but also our own selves.' The gospel was the errand; himself was thrown in. It is possible to deliver the message accurately and withhold the man, and a great deal of religious professionalism consists of exactly that — correct content, carefully rationed distance.

'Because you had become very dear to us.' That is the reason, and it is not a strategy. Paul had grown to love them, and love is what makes a person hand over more than was required. Anyone who has been served by someone who plainly liked them, as against someone discharging a duty toward them, knows the difference immediately and never forgets it.

verseByVerse.quote: For you remember, brothers, our labor and toil: we worked night and day, that we might not be a burden to any of you, while we proclaimed to you the gospel of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the verse the old quotation dropped, and it is the hardest evidence in the chapter. 'You remember, brothers, our labour and toil: we worked night and day, that we might not be a burden to any of you, while we proclaimed to you the gospel of God.'

Two words are stacked for the work. Kopos is labour to the point of exhaustion; mochthos is hardship, drudgery, the grind. Paul is not describing a trade he enjoyed. He is describing being tired.

The trade was tentmaking, or more precisely leatherworking (Acts 18:3) — heavy, unglamorous work with awl and knife, and in the ancient world manual labour was what gentlemen despised. A travelling philosopher who wanted status did not sit in a workshop. Paul sat in one, and 'night and day' means he was at the bench before dawn and after dark, with the preaching fitted around it.

Notice the reason he gives: 'that we might not be a burden to any of you.' The word means a weight laid on someone. He had just told them (v.6) that he could have made demands as an apostle. Here is what he did instead. The right existed and he paid out of his own pocket rather than use it.

And see how this answers the accusation without a word of argument. A man running a religious racket does not work a double shift to avoid taking money from his converts. The Thessalonians did not have to weigh Paul's protests about greed against somebody else's insinuations; they had watched him come to the meeting with his hands stained from the workshop.

There is a caution here against over-applying it. Paul is not laying down that ministers should never be paid — he argues the opposite at length (1 Cor 9:14; and this same letter tells the church to respect those who labour among them, 5:12). He waived a right in a particular place for a particular reason: so that nothing about money could get between these people and the gospel. What transfers is not the tentmaking but the instinct — the willingness to be out of pocket rather than let a fair claim of yours become an obstacle to somebody else's faith.

verseByVerse.quote: You are witnesses, and God also, how holy and righteous and blameless was our conduct toward you believers. For you know how, like a father with his children, we exhorted each one of you and encouraged you and charged you to walk in a manner worthy of God, who calls you into his own kingdom and glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'You are witnesses, and God also' — both courts again, the one that saw his conduct and the one that sees his heart. And three words for the conduct: holy (toward God), righteous (toward people), blameless (with nothing anyone could lay a charge on). Note the last one carefully. Paul is not claiming sinlessness; he is claiming that no accusation would stick, which is a different and testable thing.

Then the second family image, and the pair is deliberate. He was a nursing mother (v.7); now, 'like a father with his children.' The mother image carried warmth, feeding, the giving of oneself. The father image in the ancient household carried formation — the one responsible for what the child became.

Three verbs describe it. Exhorted — coming alongside to urge. Encouraged — putting heart into someone. Charged — the strongest of the three, a solemn testifying, the word for putting someone under obligation. Warmth and weight together. A father who only encourages raises children who cannot stand; one who only charges raises children who leave.

But the phrase that should stop us is 'each one of you.' In perhaps a month, in a city where he was also working night and day at a bench, Paul dealt with these people individually. He did not preach at a crowd and move on. He knew them one at a time.

And the aim of all of it: 'to walk in a manner worthy of God, who calls you into his own kingdom and glory.' Worthy is not a standard they must reach to earn something. It is a matching — conduct that fits what has happened to you, as a uniform fits the service you are in.

Notice the tense of the calling: God calls, present and ongoing. He is not only the one who called them once at conversion; he is calling them still, toward the kingdom and glory that are their destination. The walk is shaped by where it ends. And that is Paul's whole method of motivating people — not 'behave, or else', but 'this is where you are going; live like someone going there.'

verseByVerse.ref: 2:13–16 – How They Received the Word — and What It Cost
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A second thanksgiving, and it is for the manner of their hearing: they took delivery of the word and then welcomed it, not as the word of men but as what it really is, the word of God — which is at work in them still (v.13).

And that reception had a price. They became imitators of the churches in Judea, suffering the same things from their own countrymen as those churches suffered from theirs (v.14). Paul then describes the opposition he has in view: those who killed the Lord Jesus and the prophets, drove the missionaries out, displease God and oppose all mankind (v.15) by hindering the gospel from reaching the Gentiles who might be saved — so filling up the measure of their sins; and wrath has come upon them at last (v.16).
verseByVerse.theology:
Scripture as God's Own Speech

Verse 13 is one of the clearest statements in the New Testament about what Scripture is. The Thessalonians heard a leatherworker with marks on his back speaking in a rented room, and concluded they were being addressed by God. That is the decision every hearer makes, usually without noticing it. If the Bible is a valuable human document, you weigh it, keep what persuades you, and remain the judge throughout. If it is God's word, the relation reverses and it reads you. There is no third position in which it is God's word and you still hold the editorial pencil.

The consequence is the verb energeitai — at work, present and continuous. Received as human opinion the word does nothing; received as God's word it goes to work. Paul is not describing two kinds of Bible but two kinds of hearing, and the second is what produced the work of faith, labour of love and endurance he thanked God for in 1:3.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Verses 15-16 have been misused across the centuries, and their limits must be stated plainly. Paul is himself a Jew who could wish himself accursed for his kinsmen and who insists God has not rejected his people (Rom 9:3; 11:1) — whatever this passage means, it cannot mean what Romans denies. His target is named by its actions, not its race: the authorities who killed Jesus and the prophets and were then blocking the mission to the Gentiles. The charge sheet is drawn from Israel's own Scriptures, where the prophets said harder things about their nation's leadership than this — covenant rebuke spoken by an insider, which is exactly what it stops being when outsiders take it up as a weapon.

Now: 'Wrath has come upon them at last' uses a past tense for something still future — the prophetic perfect, a verdict so settled it can be announced before the sentence is carried out. And it must be read against 1:10, where wrath is precisely what Jesus delivers people from. Paul had himself been a persecutor hindering the gospel, and was rescued. A sober warning is never a licence for contempt.

verseByVerse.quote: And we also thank God constantly for this, that when you received the word of God, which you heard from us, you accepted it not as the word of men but as what it really is, the word of God, which is at work in you believers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul thanks God a second time in this letter, and what he thanks him for is not that the Thessalonians believed but how they took what they heard.

Two verbs, and the distinction between them is the point. They received the word — paralambano, the ordinary term for taking delivery of something handed to you. Then they accepted it — dechomai, to welcome, the word for taking a guest into your house. The first is hearing; the second is embracing. Plenty of people do the first every Sunday and never do the second.

And they accepted it 'not as the word of men but as what it really is, the word of God.' Weigh what that meant on the ground. They had heard it from a leatherworker with marks on his back, in a rented room, in a city full of competing lecturers. There was nothing about the delivery to compel the verdict. They looked at that and concluded they were being addressed by God.

That is the decision every hearer of Scripture makes, usually without noticing. If the Bible is a valuable human document, you weigh it, keep the parts that persuade you and set the rest aside — and you remain the judge throughout. If it is the word of God, the relation reverses and it reads you. There is no third option where it is God's word and you still hold the editorial pencil.

Then the consequence, and it is the most important clause in the verse: the word 'is at work in you believers.' The verb is energeitai — the root of our energy — and it is present and continuous. Not that the word informed them once. It is working in them now, while Paul writes.

Notice how the two halves connect, because this is the practical heart of it. Received as human opinion, the word does nothing; received as God's word, it goes to work. Paul is not describing two kinds of Bible but two kinds of hearing — and the second is the one that produced the work of faith, the labour of love and the endurance he thanked God for in chapter 1.

verseByVerse.quote: For you, brothers, became imitators of the churches of God in Christ Jesus that are in Judea. For you suffered the same things from your own countrymen as they did from the Jews,
verseByVerse.commentary:
'You became imitators of the churches of God in Judea.' In chapter 1 they became imitators of Paul and of the Lord; here of congregations a thousand miles away they had never met. And in one specific respect: 'you suffered the same things from your own countrymen as they did.'

The comparison is more carefully made than it looks. Paul does not say the Thessalonians suffered like the Judean churches in general. He matches the detail exactly — your own countrymen. The Judean believers were opposed by fellow Jews; the Thessalonian believers by fellow Greeks. In each case the opposition came not from a foreign power but from the neighbours, which is the kind that hurts most and costs most, because it is the loss of your own people.

Remember what that meant in that city. These were Gentiles who had walked out of the trade guild dinners, the household shrines and the civic festivals — the entire social fabric. The pressure would have come from employers, families, and men they had drunk with all their lives.

And Paul's purpose in drawing the parallel is pastoral. A young church under attack asks a question in the middle of the night: has something gone wrong? Did we misunderstand? Paul's answer is that they have joined a line — the same thing is happening to the oldest churches in the faith, the ones planted where Jesus himself walked. Their suffering is not evidence that they took a wrong turn. It is evidence that they are on the road.

That is worth holding onto, because it is easy to invert. Opposition is not proof of faithfulness — plenty of people are disliked for being disagreeable. But neither is it proof of failure, which is what the frightened heart assumes at three in the morning.

verseByVerse.quote: who killed both the Lord Jesus and the prophets, and drove us out, and displease God and oppose all mankind by hindering us from speaking to the Gentiles that they might be saved—so as always to fill up the measure of their sins. But wrath has come upon them at last!
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the hardest passage in the letter, and it has been misused across the centuries to justify appalling things. It must be read carefully and its limits stated plainly.

Paul describes those who 'killed both the Lord Jesus and the prophets, and drove us out, and displease God and oppose all mankind by hindering us from speaking to the Gentiles that they might be saved.'

Start with who is speaking. Paul is himself a Jew — 'of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews' (Phil 3:5) — and in Romans he writes that he could wish himself accursed for the sake of his kinsmen, and insists flatly that God has not rejected his people (Rom 9:3; 11:1). Whatever this passage means, it cannot mean what Romans denies. Nor is he condemning a race: his target is specific and he names their actions — the authorities who killed Jesus and the prophets before him, drove the missionaries out, and were at that moment blocking the gospel from reaching Gentiles.

Note too that the charge sheet is drawn from Israel's own Scriptures. The prophets said harder things about their nation's leadership than Paul does here; Jesus wept over Jerusalem for killing the prophets sent to her (Matt 23:37). This is the internal language of covenant rebuke, spoken by an insider — which is exactly what it stops being when outsiders pick it up as a weapon.

The clause 'oppose all mankind' sounds sweeping, and it is aimed at one thing: obstructing the gospel from going to the nations. To stand in the way of the only message that saves is, in Paul's reckoning, to act against humanity as such. It is a charge about the mission, not about character.

Then the last sentence: 'But wrath has come upon them at last.' The verb is past — already come. Paul most likely means that judgment is now so certain, so visibly set in motion, that it can be spoken of as arrived; within a generation Jerusalem and the temple would fall. It is the prophetic past tense, the settled verdict announced before the sentence is carried out.

And the passage must end where the letter began. Wrath is what Jesus delivers people from (1:10) — including Paul, who had himself been a persecutor of the church hindering the gospel, and was rescued. Opposition to the gospel places any people under the wrath the gospel exists to save them from, Jew or Gentile alike; and the same gospel stands open to them. A sober warning is not a licence for contempt, and anyone who has used this passage for contempt has read the man who wrote Romans 11 exactly backwards.

verseByVerse.ref: 2:17–20 – Orphaned From Them, and What He Expects to Hold
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The tone turns from defence to grief. Paul says he was orphaned from them — torn away in person though not in heart, and only for a short time — and that the separation made him try harder, not less, to see them face to face (v.17). The sentence then breaks under the pressure of feeling as he drops the plural to sign his own name: he wanted to come, again and again, but Satan cut the road (v.18).

And what is it all for? He asks what his hope, joy and crown of boasting will be before the Lord Jesus at his coming, and answers his own question — is it not you? (v.19). Then plainly, in the present tense: you are our glory and joy (v.20).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Coming, and the Pastor's Wreath

Verse 19 brings in parousia for the first time in the letter. In ordinary Greek it named the state visit of a sovereign to one of his cities: the citizens streaming out to meet him on the road and escorting him in. The Thessalonians had watched such arrivals. Paul takes that civic vocabulary and applies it to the return of Jesus — and will use the same picture again in 4:17.

The stephanos fits the same scene. It is not the royal diadem but the wreath given to a victor at the games, and also placed on a dignitary honoured at a royal visit. So the picture is the King arriving, and Paul standing there — with nothing to show but a group of people. Their being there is the wreath. It is among the most moving statements in the New Testament about what pastoral work is finally for: the reward is not the admiration of the present age but the sight, on that day, of people standing before Jesus because the gospel was faithfully preached and patiently tended.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: We are not told how Satan hindered him. It may have been the bond the magistrates took from Jason (Acts 17:9), which would have made Paul's return dangerous for his hosts. What matters is how he read it: not as bad luck and not as God saying no, but as an enemy with an interest in keeping a young church from its teacher. The verb enekopsen was used of breaking up a road to stop an army.

Now: Hold that carefully in both directions. Not everything that goes wrong is a demonic assault, and a Christian who reads every delay that way will end up exhausted and superstitious. But Paul plainly did not regard his frustrations as merely administrative. And note what he never says — that Satan won. Timothy went in his place (3:2), and this letter exists because Paul could not come, which is a fair accounting of who was hindered in the end. Verse 19 also supplies the test for motives: on the last day, is what you expect to hold up a record of what you achieved, or people who are standing there because of it?

verseByVerse.quote: But since we were torn away from you, brothers, for a short time, in person not in heart, we endeavored the more eagerly and with great desire to see you face to face, because we wanted to come to you—I, Paul, again and again—but Satan hindered us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tone changes completely. 'Since we were torn away from you, brothers, for a short time, in person not in heart.'

'Torn away' is aporphanisthentes, and it is built on the word for orphan. Paul says he was orphaned from them. He has just called himself their mother and their father; now, with the images reversed, he is the bereaved one — the parent who has lost the children. It is an extraordinary thing for a grown man to write about a congregation he had known for a matter of weeks.

Two qualifications keep the grief from being despair. 'For a short time' — the separation is temporary, whatever it feels like. And 'in person not in heart' — literally in face, not in heart. The distance is physical only.

Then the effort: 'we endeavoured the more eagerly and with great desire to see you face to face.' Note that being torn away made him try harder rather than settle into resignation. And the sentence breaks apart under the pressure of feeling in verse 18 — 'because we wanted to come to you — I, Paul, again and again —'. He interrupts his own plural to sign his own name. Whoever else may have been prevented, he wants them to know that he tried, repeatedly.

'But Satan hindered us.' The verb enekopsen means to cut into, and it was used of breaking up a road to stop an army's advance. Something was put across the way.

Paul does not tell us the mechanism, and it is worth being honest that we do not know: it may have been the bond the magistrates took from Jason (Acts 17:9), which would have made Paul's return dangerous for his hosts, or illness, or hostility elsewhere. What matters is how he read it. He does not treat the obstruction as bad luck or as God saying no; he names an enemy with an interest in keeping a young church away from its teacher.

Hold that with care, in both directions. Not everything that goes wrong is a demonic assault, and a Christian who reads every delay that way will be exhausted and superstitious. But Paul plainly did not believe that his frustrations were merely administrative. And notice what he never says: that Satan won. Timothy went instead (3:2), and the letter you are reading was written because Paul could not come — which is not a bad accounting of who was hindered in the end.

verseByVerse.quote: For what is our hope or joy or crown of boasting before our Lord Jesus at his coming? Is it not you? For you are our glory and joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul has been defending himself against the charge of chasing glory (v.6). Now, at the end of the chapter, he says what he is actually after — and the answer is the people he is writing to.

'What is our hope or joy or crown of boasting before our Lord Jesus at his coming? Is it not you?' He asks it as a question and answers it himself, and the effect is warmer than a statement would have been.

The 'crown' is stephanos — not the royal diadem but the wreath of leaves put on the head of the winner at the games. And in Thessalonica the image had a second edge: such a wreath was also placed on a dignitary who was honoured when a king or emperor visited the city. That is precisely the scene Paul is describing.

Because 'at his coming' is parousia, and this is the word's first appearance in the letter. In ordinary Greek it meant the state visit of a sovereign to one of his cities — the citizens streaming out to meet him on the road and escorting him in. The Thessalonians would have watched such an arrival. Paul takes the civic vocabulary of a Roman world and applies it to the return of Jesus, and he will use the same picture again in chapter 4.

So the picture is this: the King arrives, and Paul is standing there — and what he has to show is not a record of his labours but a group of people. Their being there is the wreath.

Then verse 20, stripped of the imagery and said plainly: 'For you are our glory and joy.' Present tense. Not only will be, on that day — are, now, while he is separated from them and unable to get back.

And this settles the accusation of the chapter better than any of the denials. A man seeking glory from people uses them and moves on. Paul's glory is them. Anyone in any kind of Christian work can test their own motives against it: on the last day, is what you expect to hold up a record of what you achieved, or a group of people who are standing there because of it?

2.text: <sup>1</sup>For you yourselves know, brothers, that our coming to you was not in vain.<sup>2</sup>But though we had already suffered and been shamefully treated at Philippi, as you know, we had boldness in our God to declare to you the gospel of God in the midst of much conflict.<sup>3</sup>For our appeal does not spring from error or impurity or any attempt to deceive,<sup>4</sup>but just as we have been approved by God to be entrusted with the gospel, so we speak, not to please man, but to please God who tests our hearts.<sup>5</sup>For we never came with words of flattery, as you know, nor with a pretext for greed—God is witness.<sup>6</sup>Nor did we seek glory from people, whether from you or from others, though we could have made demands as apostles of Christ.<sup>7</sup>But we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother taking care of her own children.<sup>8</sup>So, being affectionately desirous of you, we were ready to share with you not only the gospel of God but also our own selves, because you had become very dear to us.<sup>9</sup>For you remember, brothers, our labor and toil: we worked night and day, that we might not be a burden to any of you, while we proclaimed to you the gospel of God.<sup>10</sup>You are witnesses, and God also, how holy and righteous and blameless was our conduct toward you believers.<sup>11</sup>For you know how, like a father with his children,<sup>12</sup>we exhorted each one of you and encouraged you and charged you to walk in a manner worthy of God, who calls you into his own kingdom and glory.<sup>13</sup>And we also thank God constantly for this, that when you received the word of God, which you heard from us, you accepted it not as the word of men but as what it really is, the word of God, which is at work in you believers.<sup>14</sup>For you, brothers, became imitators of the churches of God in Christ Jesus that are in Judea. For you suffered the same things from your own countrymen as they did from the Jews,<sup>15</sup>who killed both the Lord Jesus and the prophets, and drove us out, and displease God and oppose all mankind<sup>16</sup>by hindering us from speaking to the Gentiles that they might be saved—so as always to fill up the measure of their sins.
